content.title: AI Coach vs Human Coach: Which One You Need and When
content.definition: AI coach vs human coach is a fit decision, not a ranking: an AI coach gives unlimited, low-cost, always-available structure for planning, preparation and follow-through, while a human coach brings relationship depth, judgment about people and accountability to another person. Most high performers need the AI for daily cadence and a human for rare, high-stakes moments.

question_sections.question: When does an AI coach beat a human coach?
question_sections.answer: When the need is frequency: daily planning, preparing for a meeting tonight, recovering after a missed day or reviewing the week. An AI coach is available at 6 a.m. and costs the same on the fiftieth session as on the first, so it wins wherever cadence matters more than relationship.

question_sections.question: When does a human coach still win?
question_sections.answer: When the problem is about people or identity: a co-founder conflict, a board relationship, a career transition or anything emotionally loaded. A human reads what you are not saying and holds you accountable as a person; a model cannot carry that weight.

question_sections.answer: It is coaching where a platform matches you with a human coach based on your goals and profile, usually through an employer program; BetterUp and CoachHub work this way. AI coaching is different: no human is assigned and the system itself runs the sessions.

content.title: Review Cadence Meaning: Daily, Weekly and Quarterly Reviews
content.definition: Review cadence means the fixed schedule on which you look back at your work and decide what changes: a short daily close, a weekly review of priorities and commitments, and a monthly or quarterly review of goals. A good cadence is set in advance and kept regardless of mood, so drift is caught within days rather than months.

question_sections.question: What is a good review cadence?
question_sections.answer: Daily: 5-10 minutes to close the day and set tomorrow's first action. Weekly: 30-45 minutes to compare commitments with what happened and choose next week's one priority. Quarterly: 60-90 minutes to check goals against results and drop what no longer matters.

question_sections.question: Why does review cadence matter more than the review template?
question_sections.answer: Because a review that happens on schedule catches drift while it is still cheap to fix. Most systems fail not because the template is wrong but because reviews are skipped after a bad week, which is exactly when they are needed.

question_sections.question: How do you keep a review cadence after missing one?
question_sections.answer: Do the next scheduled review, not a catch-up. Skip the backlog, review only the current week and apply never-miss-twice: one missed review is noise, two in a row is the signal to shorten the review rather than abandon it.

facts: Working lengths: daily close 5-10 minutes, weekly review 30-45 minutes, quarterly review 60-90 minutes.

faq.question: What does review cadence mean?
faq.answer: Review cadence is how often, and on what fixed schedule, you review your work and plans - for example a daily close, a weekly review and a quarterly reset. The cadence is the rhythm; the review is what you do inside it.

faq.question: What is a review cadence?

faq.question: What does cadence review mean?
faq.answer: A cadence review checks the cadence itself: whether your daily, weekly and quarterly reviews are actually happening and are the right length. Review cadence is the schedule; a cadence review audits it.
